From the Chair 3 This is my last article in our magazine as chair, and my last address will be to our AGM on the 10th September. It's always good to get together, and I can look back at many happy u3a memories of the last couple of years: • new groups and group leaders • new teams and team members – including our committee • new systems and payment methods • new members—and I’m encouraged to see so many joining online now • new ways of being together, including Events • an open day, where over 300 people visited • Thank you days for volunteers. We can look forward to even more happening in coming years, and I look forward myself to being part of that, if not as chair. I know many see the dark side of AI, but I'm particularly passionate about understanding what AI can do for us and in using it effectively. (If you want to know more, I have lots of examples - just say Buses, Beacon, or Cemeteries to me!). Please do remember that we are all able to contribute to our life in the u3a, and we rely on each other to contribute as we are all volunteers. We are free to do almost anything (legal) that we want, that can help us to meet and “learn, laugh, live”. We're limited only by our imaginations, and our capacity - and there is lots of support. So thanks again to everybody who contributes in any way to our life together, and I look forward to seeing you at the AGM when we'll be electing our new committee. By the way, some of you have asked what I'll be doing with “all my spare time” (!), and I can honestly say that I'll be carrying on doing a lot of what I am doing now - aiming to gradually hand over much of it to others. But I also have one or two big projects that I've been working on, and I'm looking forward to spending more time on them. Best wishes Peter
Members ’ Open Meetings All Members’ Open Meetings are held at the Corn Exchange, St Ives 1.20pm for 2.00pm start. Please note: We kindly ask that members wishing to discuss membership matters or to book outings or theatre trips please arrive early to avoid disruption. Committee members and the Group Support Team will be available after the meeting to answer questions and discuss any matters of concern. A full list of this year’s Open Meetings: u3aivo.uk/monthly 4 Thursday 10th September AGM—see page 5 Gardening for Wildlife Speaker: Sue Jones Thursday 8 th October The Life, Music and Inﬂuence of Buddy Holly Speaker: Tony Tutton Tony Tutton will take you on a journey through the life of the legendary Buddy Holly from his birthplace in Lubbock Texas in 1936 to his untimely death on 3rd February 1959. The talk features many of Buddy smash hits, That’ll be the day, Oh Boy, Peggy Sue, Rave on, Heartbeat …and lots more. Hear songs from many artists that inﬂuenced Buddy such as Hank Williams, Johnny Cash, Elvis, Carl Perkins, Jerry Lee Lewis, Bill Haley & His Comets. Thursday 12 th November Wing Commander T H Baker DFC DFM Speaker: Helen Baker A talk honouring the experiences of Tom Baker whilst a POW in Stalag Luft III, the scene of the Great Escape, and of the long march home. Told by his granddaughter Helen Cooper, the daughter of Peter Baker the ﬁrst chairman of St Ives u3a.
5 Our Next Members ’ Open Meeting Our Members ’ Open Meeting on Thursday 10th September will begin at 2pm with our AGM and you have already been sent notice of this meeting, along with relevant papers. It is anticipated this will be a short meeting, mainly to appoint officers and trustees for another year, and to receive last year ’ s financial report. This year ’ s committee and other posts are listed below. See u3aivo.uk/agm . If you cannot actually come to the AGM in person but still want to play your part, you can vote by “ proxy ”. It is your way of being present and telling the chair how to place your votes. This year ’ s proxy form is attached with this magazine and available on the website. You need to get the signed form to the Secretary no later than 10am on Tuesday 8th September, either to 20 West Leys, St Ives, PE27 6DS, or secretarystivescambsu3a@gmail.com . We encourage proxy voting by any member who is unable to attend in person as this not only enables you to share in our decision - making, but also means you are included in the numbers that go towards the quorum for the meeting. 6 Christmas Carol Goes Wrong Wednesday 3rd February Milton Keynes Theatre As the Cornley crew hilariously battle miscommunication, delays to their set, actors missing in action and a growing feud over who will play the lead, it’s sure to be a disastrous take on the much-loved classic Christmas story of Ebeneezer Scrooge. Will Cornley ﬁnally change their ways, or will their misfortunes wreak havoc with hysterical consequences. Enjoy a festive slice of pure escapism at the worst production in Christmas past, present and yet to come! Don’t be a Scrooge, book now. Victoria Wood’s Dinnerladies Wednesday 17th March Milton Keynes Theatre Without doubt one of the classic television sitcoms of the late ‘90s, Victoria Wood’s Dinnerladies starred Wood as Brenda Furlong, a worker in the canteen of a factory in Manchester, surrounded by a cast of characters covering the gamut of types you’d expect in there – chain smoking canteen manager Tony, fellow Dinnerladies Dolly, Twinkle, Jean and Anita, wise caretaker Stan and other loveable characters. Taking direct inspiration from storylines in the beloved TV series, the stage adaptation is the perfect way to revisit the classic. Starring Les Dennis. u3a ’ s Got Talent u3a’s Got Talent Friday 16th October 7pm St Ives Corn Exchange Another ﬁrst venture for our Events Team is ‘u3a’s Got Talent – an evening of music and art’ to be held on Friday 16th October in St Ives Corn Exchange. Don’t worry – no judging will be involved! We will be hearing performances from our various musical and singing groups, interspersed with a few contributions from the Creative Writing Group. We have also invited our art and handicraft groups to bring some samples of their work to display. Doors will open at 6.30pm when Jazz Combo will be playing as people arrive, and there will be the opportunity to wander round and look at the art and craft work. The programme will begin at 7pm when groups taking part will include Classical Guitar, Uke-Troupe, Jazz Combo, Singing for Pleasure, and our recently formed Signing Choir, supported by members from Guitar Club. The Riverport Bar will be open for purchase of drinks, and during the interval there will be a further opportunity to take a look at the art and craft work on display. The event is open to St Ives u3a members only and tickets will cost £5. Any member taking part in the performance or bringing work to display can pay a reduced entrance fee of £3 but, to ease the burden on Sue who processes all the event bookings, group leaders have been asked to block -book tickets for their groups. For other members wishing to book a ticket, please visit the Events web page here: u3aivo.uk/events We hope this will be an opportunity for our members to enjoy hearing and seeing something of what goes on in our varied group activities week by week. 8

These bespoke trips have been designed to create opportunities for members to come together from across the UK to learn, discover and explore. Every getaway blends relaxed, well-organised travel with enriching and immersive experiences. Beyond traditional sightseeing, you can expect talks, workshops and shared adventures that build lasting friendships. They have teamed up with The UK Holiday Group, a highly respected name in travel with over 40 years’ expertise in creating exceptional excursions. The main aim of our group is to have fun working with fabrics, threads and dyes alongside like- minded people who enjoy experimenting and creating. For us ‘Textiles’ includes the dyeing and printing of fabrics and the creation of artwork, home furnishings and/or garments, through hand and machine stitching. Members often bring a wealth of experience, having developed a variety of skills over the years. We share this knowledge, and enthusiasm, as we work on our individual projects. You are also very welcome to join us if you’re new to Textiles. Our monthly demonstrations may even inspire your own creative projects. During the ﬁrst two years we have tried a range of creative methods such as: silk painting, free-machine stitching, trapping ﬁbres and threads between sheer fabrics, painting directly onto fabrics with fabric paints, creating texture with Applique and reverse Applique, ice -dyeing with tied and distorted fabric, machining onto soluble fabrics, use of Angelina ﬁbres, plus Nuno-felting. The ﬁnal two techniques were introduced and demonstrated by group members. This epitomises one of the strengths of the u3a: sharing knowledge and skills with one another. I hope we can build on this approach in the future. We have each chosen our own design inspiration from These is using the layer, paint and stitch technique and are of Cley Windmill and blue turkey tail mushrooms by Caroline Pye Spotlight on Textiles 14 The quarterly magazine has the space to look at group activities more closely. In this issue we hear about Anne Guinea ’s Textile Group and the beautiful work the members have produced. Abstracts, embellished textured materials by Christine Myles
15 photographs, books, artists, and nature. Then produced our own sketches before testing and sampling the techniques that will suit the design proposal. In the year ahead we aim to develop our range of skills to include lino-printing, screen- printing, several types of quilting, spray-dyeing, plus pleating and gathering to create texture. Group members can opt out of the demonstrations and focus on producing their own unique ﬁnished pieces. As a result, the meetings are relaxed and ﬂexible. The photographs show just some of the beautiful textiles produced by the group. The group currently has eleven members and one free space, so come along and have some fun with fabrics! If you would like to give creative Textiles a try, please contact me via the website. Anne Guinea Christmas decoration with sheer fabric and free sewing. 18 Model Aeroplanes by Garry Flack I have been aero modelling for the last 37 years and I joined the Impington Village College model aeroplane club in 1990. The club has just celebrated its 80th Birthday. It was founded by the Art master Ray Malmsrom on his return from the RAF in 1946. It was for boys of the school and at that time called the Flying Squadron. Over the years I have tried most disciplines, control line (model controlled using steel wires) radio control, indoor and outdoor free ﬂight, either engine or rubber band powered. It may be of interest to understand what these strange characters get up to with pieces of balsa wood, tissue paper and sometimes plastic foam. Indoor Free Flight Scale I would like to touch on free ﬂight scale models particularly indoor free ﬂight scale. These models are usually ﬂown in a hall and often in a large gymnasium hired for the purpose especially for competitions. Models for indoor competition must be built using a published plan or be researched, designed and built by the competitors. Documentation has to be submitted to prove the accuracy of the model to the real thing. Models are statically judged for accuracy and skill of the builder. The model has to be “trimmed” to ﬂy within the conﬁnes of the hall and is judged for takeoff, landing, realistic speed and often duration of ﬂight. The models I have ﬂown indoors have all been powered by a propeller driven by a wound up rubber band, we call it a “rubber motor”, because it uses a special rubber cut to size and ends tied to form a loop. Bear in mind that some of these motors are wound with up to 1500 turns, are usually a loop twice the length of the fuselage and models can ﬂy in a circle for more than 60 seconds. The model has to be trimmed to ﬂy in a circle by tweaking the rudder and other controls on the model, to achieve a good ﬂight. It’s a bit of a black art, can be frustrating and yet very rewarding when it ﬂies well without hitting anything. Some are easy to ﬂy and some never make it, quite happy to destroy themselves by hitting everything in site, like a death wish. You never know. In the end you make the adjustments, wind the model up and just let it go. Here are three examples of models entered into three different classes in free ﬂight scale competitions over the last few years…...
19 Kit Scale Class Aronca Champion aircraft It had to be constructed from a published plan, judged for skill and accuracy to the plan. You are allowed three ﬂight attempts, judged on take off ,cruise and landing. Constructed with traditional materials of balsa and tissue. Pistachio Scale Class (originated in the USA) Can be your own design with maximum wingspan of 8 inches. Judged statically, points awarded, nine attempts at ﬂight duration the best 2 counting for points. This model constructed from insulation foam, off cuts from a building site, and painted to represent a Westland Wyvern ﬁghter bomber that was used during the Suez crisis. Various stages of construction shown to the completed model. All up weight 5.5 grams. This model was a winner on two occasions. Peanut Scale Class (originated in USA) To have a maximum wingspan of 11 inches and judging is the same as the Pistachio class. This model also made from insulation foam and everything constructed by myself. This is a model of a German WW2 ﬁghter the Focke-wolf FW190 D9. It is very stable and ﬂies well. I hope this has been of interest and explains some of what I do in my spare time, Bowls, Art and u3a take up the rest.! Garry Flack

St Ives Repair Cafe Maybe you’ve noticed the brightly coloured posters around town publicising the next pop- up Repair café on the afternoon of the 17th October in the Methodist Church and wondered what it’s all about. If you have a broken toaster lurking at the back of the cupboard, a radio that doesn’t work, blunt secateurs or just a pair of pyjamas that need new elastic, dig them out and bring them along. You’ll ﬁnd a team of repairers with all sorts of expertise waiting to have a go at mending your item and saving it from landﬁll. An average of 40 or so items are repaired during the course of an afternoon, ranging from vintage clocks, broken toys or china ornaments, record players, broken zips to bicycles and all sorts of electrical goods. A pair of binoculars with a broken wheel was booked into one café; one of the repairers had brought along a 3D printer and was able to produce a new wheel, much to the delight of the owner! If an item cannot be mended advice will be given as to whether a spare part should be purchased or it really has reached the end of its life. A limited number of appointments can be booked or simply come along and take your item to be assessed by one of our experts. Whilst waiting for a repairer to come available you can enjoy a cuppa and homemade cake. Since October 2022 the event has been put on three times a year, all run by volunteers (including a fair few u3a members) giving freely of their time and expertise. I have been helping since the ﬁrst café and thoroughly enjoy being involved. If you’d like to join our team or to book an item in for repair, contact me on stivesrepaircafe@gmail.com Sheila Louth 21

Images from the ‘St Ives 100 Years Ago’ Photo Album https://www.facebook.com/stives100yearsago Market Hill in 1901 on a Monday market day. The newly erected statue of Oliver Cromwell (1901) is just visible. By this date the new cattle market had opened (1866) and the Bullock Market renamed the Broadway. Every Monday St Ives was crammed with 12,000 beasts of all descriptions, ﬂooding into a town of 3,000 inhabitants. The Royal Scots Greys in 1912, riding from Hemingford Meadow down Bridge Street. They were deployed to France in August 1914, immediately serving as a vital rearguard shield during the gruelling Retreat from Mons.
